items.description: Πρώτον, τα καλά νέα: Ο κόσμος μπορεί να είναι πολύ πιο κοντά από ό,τι πιστεύουμε σε έναν διεθνή στόχο προστασίας του 30% της γης έως το 2030. Τα κακά νέα: Μάλλον δεν είναι η σωστή γη. Τα έθνη του κόσμου έχουν θέσει προστασία στο 27% περίπου των χερσαίων μαζών του πλανήτη, πολύ περισσότερο από το 19% που πιστευόταν προηγουμένως, σύμφωνα με έρευνα που δημοσιεύθηκε πρόσφατα…
items.descriptionOriginal: First, the good news: The world might be a lot closer than we think to an international goal of protecting 30% of land by 2030. The bad news: It’s probably not all the right land. The nations of the world have placed protections on roughly 27% of the planet’s land masses, far more than the 19% previously thought, according to research recently published in Nature . There has been much hand wringing among conservation-minded folks that countries were woefully behind on land protection pledges made in 2022 to shield 30% of Earth’s land and 30% of the ocean from development as part of an update to the Convention on Biological Diversity, the main international agreement aimed at the current extinction crisis. But “our analysis suggests that much more of the land is in some type of conservation area than currently recognized,” said lead author Helen O’Neill, a postdoctoral researcher at the United Kingdom’s Institute of Zoology, London. The official tally tracking protected lands is a database at the Protected Planet website , a collaboration between the United Nations and the International Union for Conservation of Nature. While this is the authoritative source, it’s incomplete. Some protected land hasn’t been registered there by countries. And it doesn’t include significant acreage that falls into a kind of gray area – land that isn’t formally protected chiefly for wildlife, but where regulations provide many of the same benefits. Known as “other effective area-based conservation measures” or OECMs, this might include land protected as sacred by Indigenous groups or managed to improve water quality. O’Neill and 35 other scientists from across the globe set out to tally this overlooked land to create a more complete picture. To reduce the massive effort required to scrutinize the status of every piece of land on the planet, the researcher selected pieces totaling 10% of all the world’s land masses. That included terrain scattered across the world and covering major types of ecosystems, from the Rocky Mountains in Montana to the Amazonian jungle to the desert of the Arabian Peninsula. .IRPP_ruby where regulations and management practices made them good candidates for being OECMs. The scientists used the results to create a computer model that estimated how this pattern would apply to the entire world. The result was the encouraging estimate that 26.8% of all land is protected, at least on paper. But that doesn’t mean conservationists can cruise across the 2030 finish line with their arms raised. Because the research also revealed troubling holes in where these lands are being conserved. Of the 173 different ecological regions scientists have mapped around the world, fewer than 100 have greater than 17% of their land protected, the scientists estimated. Regions that are primarily ice and rock – polar and alpine landscapes – are significantly overrepresented in the catalog of protected areas. That’s not a big surprise, since those regions are often less attractive for human settlement or exploitation by farming or other activities. By contrast, deserts, woodlands, grasslands and temperate forests all fall below the 30% target. Then there is the question of whether land that’s conserved on paper is really being protected . The new research points to the potential gains that can be made, particularly with the recognition of the conservation potential of these OECMs. But “conserving 30% of land and seas is not sufficient on its own,” said Heather Bingham, a co-author who heads the Protected Planet Initiative. “The target also calls for these areas to be managed effectively for positive biodiversity outcomes, and to be placed where they will have the greatest impact on biodiversity.” O’Neill, et. al. “ Global conservation area coverage substantially exceeds current estimates .” Nature. items.descriptionOriginal: At Joy Durga Bhandar, a workshop in north Kolkata's Kumartuli, Koushik Ghosh begins an idol with a framework of bamboo and wood tied together with jute rope. From this base come the sculpted figures, decorations and layers of colour that devotees see during Durga Puja. Koushik knows this process well. For generations, artisans in Kumartuli have worked with bamboo, straw and clay, shaping idols by hand for Kolkata's Durga Puja celebrations. Over time, many workshops also adopted thermocol decorations, synthetic paints and plastic ornaments because they were quicker or cheaper to use. Koushik is looking for ways to bring more traditional materials back into his work. "The frame, the clay, the straw, those were always ours. The thermocol and the chemical colours came later, because they were cheaper and faster. I am going back to what was here before," he says. The straw framework gives the idol its shape before artisans add the first layers of clay. He is working towards idols decorated with natural clay, shola (the soft pith of a plant used for delicate ornaments) and natural colours instead of thermocol. Every year, after Durga Puja, thousands of idols are immersed in the Hooghly River and other water bodies. In 2025, around 5,200 idols were immersed across 34 major Hooghly ghats and approximately 30 other water bodies in Kolkata and nearby suburbs, according to The Times of India . Civic workers clear debris from immersion sites, but thermocol and plastic decorations need careful collection and disposal because they can persist in the environment. Neel, a volunteer who has spent several seasons cleaning the Hooghly's banks near Babughat, remembers finding thermocol floating on the surface, coloured residue near the banks, and plastic decorations gathering along the ghats. Kumartuli's workshops have produced clay idols for Kolkata's Durga Puja for generations. For Koushik, the challenge is to make the decorations less wasteful while keeping the craft affordable for the families who depend on it. From bamboo frames to Durga's eyes: Inside the craft of Kumartuli Walking through Kumartuli's narrow lanes, the smell of wet clay is difficult to miss. The neighbourhood, whose name comes from kumor (potter) and tuli (neighbourhood quarter), has been home to idol makers for more than three centuries. Its workshops stand between Rabindra Sarani and the Hooghly, the river that has long supplied the fine alluvial soil used in their craft. Traditionally known as Ganga maati , this clay is softer and finer than ordinary earth, allowing artisans to sculpt delicate features. Artisans shape clay over the bamboo-and-straw framework before adding finer details and colour. At Koushik's workshop, everything begins with the kathamo (a framework made from bamboo and wood). "The frame is not just engineering," he explains. "It is the first thing she stands on." The structure must support the central Durga figure, accompanying figures, a lion and other sculpted elements. Next comes khar bandha (tying straw around the frame). Carefully shaped bundles of straw form the arms, waist, chest and other features. If the straw is tied incorrectly, the figure may lose its balance or the clay may crack. The first clay layer is entel mati (sticky clay mixed with tush , or rice husk). It takes about three to four days to dry. Straw and clay form the idol's limbs, which must be balanced before the finer layers are applied. Artisans then apply bele mati (finer, smoother clay), allowing another five or six days for drying, depending on the weather. Any cracks are repaired with fresh mud. Faces, hands and other delicate parts are often made separately using chhach (moulds), helping workshops manage the large number of orders they receive. The final detailing includes chokkhudaan (painting the eyes). Some artisans specialise in this stage because even a slight difference in the brushstrokes can change the expression of the figure. This process has remained largely familiar across generations. A Durga idol includes accompanying figures and a lion, all assembled before the final decoration. The changes have come in the materials used for decoration and finishing. Earlier, artisans relied on bamboo, straw, jute, shola and natural pigments. Tamarind-seed gum, chalk powder and starch made from boiled arrowroot were used to prepare and finish colours. As demand grew, thermocol became popular for chaal (decorative backdrops), mukut (crowns) and ornaments. Synthetic paints offered brighter colours, while plastic jewellery entered some workshops. These alternatives were quicker, cheaper and easier to work with when deadlines were approaching. The extra work behind a natural finish Gopal, a veteran artisan who remembers making idols before thermocol became common, understands why workshops adopted it. He recalls decorating traditional sabeki pratima (traditional-style idols) with shola, cloth, zari and daaker saaj (traditional decorative work). Handmade clay figures require repeated shaping and drying, adding to an artisan's working hours. "Shola was beautiful, but it took time. Thermocol came because it was fast and cheap. If you remove thermocol now and don't give me shola at the same price and within the same time, I am just working slower for the same money," he says. Thermocol is lightweight, easy to cut and relatively inexpensive. Shola, jute, handmade paper, paper pulp, bamboo and clay ornaments may require more time and skill, and sometimes cost more. Natural colours create another difficulty. Asha, who manages colouring and finishing work at a Kumartuli studio, says buyers have grown accustomed to the bright, uniform finish of synthetic paints. "Natural colour is more beautiful if you know how to look at it. But the buyer is standing under LED lights in the pandal. They want brightness. Softness looks like less work to them, even when it is more," she explains. Colouring and decoration come after sculpting, with buyers often expecting a bright, even finish. This expectation has financial consequences. Koushik points to raw-material prices, labour, drying time and the risk of damage as factors that can raise the cost of working with natural materials. Handmade decorations take more hours. Natural colours need careful application. During the monsoon, wet clay can also take longer to dry. In the final weeks of a season, artisans often work long hours to meet delivery dates, using fans and tarpaulins to manage damp conditions. Koushik has not lost an idol to rain, but the possibility remains with every order that needs additional drying time. Artisans use fans and tarpaulins to manage damp conditions while working to Puja deadlines. The bigger challenge is recovering these expenses. There is no fixed price for a Durga idol. The cost depends on its height, design, decorations, arrangement of figures and the buyer's budget. Even two idols of the same height can have different prices. Costs differ by design, materials and year, so there is no single price difference between idols using natural decorations and those made with synthetic alternatives. For a small workshop, even a modest unplanned expense can make a difference. "If the idol has to be eco-friendly and the client wants the same finish as a synthetic-painted one, one of us has to absorb the difference. Usually, it is us," Asha says. The cost of an idol depends on its size, design, decorative materials and time spent finishing it. A South Kolkata Puja committee organiser, who requested anonymity, describes the buyer's dilemma. His committee relies on contributions from neighbourhood families, so any increase in an idol's price or change in its appearance must be discussed with the people paying for it. Gopal believes buyers and artisans should agree on materials and costs when placing an order. That would help workshops plan their purchases without bearing unexpected expenses themselves. After the idols are immersed, what is left in the Hooghly? Idol immersion is an important part of Durga Puja. The environmental concern lies with synthetic decorations and paints that may enter the water or be left on the banks unless they are removed and collected. Thermocol and plastic do not biodegrade easily and can break into smaller fragments that remain in the environment. Some synthetic paints contain heavy metals that can affect water quality. Decorative paints and plastic ornaments may leave residues that require post-immersion collection. A Central Pollution Control Board study conducted between 1993 and 1995 estimated that idol immersions released 32 tonnes of colours and 16.8 tonnes of varnish and garjan oil annually into the Hooghly during that period. These colours contained metals including lead, mercury and chromium, according to findings reported by Down To Earth . These are historical findings, not a measure of present-day pollution. They help explain why safer materials and careful post-immersion clean-ups matter. The CPCB's revised guidelines of May 2020 call for natural, biodegradable idols, discourage toxic synthetic paints and restrict thermocol, plastic and plaster of Paris. CPCB guidelines favour biodegradable idols and discourage thermocol, plastic and toxic paints. West Bengal's 2018 immersion rules require natural clay and bamboo, prohibit plaster of Paris and toxic colours, and place responsibilities on Puja committees and local authorities. Decorative thermocol has also been prohibited under national single-use plastic restrictions effective from July 2022. For workshops, switching materials works best when decisions are made before production begins. In August 2025, The Times of India reported that police were conducting awareness drives and inspections at Kumartuli and other idol-making centres. West Bengal's immersion rules call for natural clay and bamboo and prohibit toxic colours. Artisans interviewed for that report asked for guidance six to eight months before Durga Puja, when orders and material choices can still be changed. Koushik agrees that natural decorations need to be planned from the start. A 25-YO idol maker puts paper pulp & plant colours to the test A few workshops have already begun experimenting with alternatives. Ritwik, a 25-year-old third-generation idol maker, has been testing paper pulp for ornaments and plant-based colours for the faces of idols. After attending an awareness workshop, he brought back samples of gerua (an earth-based red pigment), turmeric-based colours and dyes derived from plants. He began trying them on small clay surfaces before using them on larger figures. "The look is different. Not worse, actually; I think it is more beautiful. But it is older-looking. Some clients like that. Some think I made a mistake. It depends on whether they know what they are seeing," he says. Artisans testing plant-based pigments say their finishes can look different from synthetic paints. The softer, slightly uneven appearance resembles the finish of traditional idols made before synthetic paints became widespread. There is no reliable figure for how many Kumartuli workshops have completely moved away from thermocol. During the reporter's visits, thermocol decorations and synthetic paints were still visible in workshops. Experiments with natural alternatives were promising, but had yet to become the norm. With thousands of idols made in Kumartuli each season, these material choices can add up. According to a September 2026 report in The Telegraph , around 166 studios produce close to 8,500 idols in a season, with turnover exceeding ₹200 crore in the previous year. A 2026 report estimated around 166 Kumartuli studios making close to 8,500 idols each season. Koushik and other artisans say a broader shift will depend on affordable traditional materials, clear specifications from buyers and guidance shared well before production begins. A reliable supply of shola, jute and natural pigments would also make it easier for workshops to plan ahead. What a painted tile shows about the choice At Gopal's workshop, a painted tile offers another way to compare the materials. One strip was coloured with synthetic paint, the other with natural pigment. Gopal left both exposed through the previous monsoon to see how they changed. The synthetic strip remained uniform; the natural one developed warmer, slightly uneven edges. Gopal did not declare either better. For him, the contrast shows how a natural finish may differ from what buyers are accustomed to. Natural pigments can create a different finish, while handmade ornaments take time. These differences need to be part of the discussion when an idol is commissioned. Traditional clay figures are moulded and dried before receiving their colours and decorations. Koushik is working to bring more of the materials his craft has long relied on back into use. Buyers can help by agreeing on materials and budgets early; timely guidance and access to affordable supplies could help more workshops do the same. Behind every idol are weeks of skilled labour. Choices about paint, decorations and post-immersion waste collection matter both to the artisans and to the river near their workshops. For Koushik, the goal is practical: honour an old craft, reduce the amount of synthetic waste entering the Hooghly and make sure artisans can still earn a fair living. Αλλά στην Almora του Uttarakhand, ένας καινοτόμος έχει περάσει 13 χρόνια δουλεύοντας για μια παρόμοια ιδέα, οδηγούμενος από ένα πρόβλημα πολύ πιο κοντά στο σπίτι. Ο Ράβι Τάμτα μεγάλωσε στο βουνό…
items.descriptionOriginal: Flying cars are once again taking over the internet, with Tesla's plans fuelling conversations about a future where people could travel through the air instead of sitting in traffic. But in Almora, Uttarakhand, an innovator has spent 13 years working towards a similar idea, driven by a problem much closer to home. Ravi Tamta grew up in the mountains of Kaflikhan village near Jageswar Dham, where reaching a hospital could mean hours on winding roads. He began wondering if there was another way to travel through the hills, one that did not depend on roads or require an airport. Inspired by the challenges of reaching hospitals in the hills, Ravi Tamta spent 13 years developing a flying vehicle that can take off and land vertically. Photograph: ( Zee News) That question led him to build HAPIDA SKYNeX, an electric flying vehicle prototype that can take off and land vertically. After years of experiments, the vehicle completed its maiden test flight in August, taking off from an army helipad in Almora and remaining airborne for nearly a minute. A mountain problem sparked the idea For people living in hilly regions, distance is not always measured in kilometres. Winding roads and difficult terrain can turn a relatively short journey into a long trip, particularly when someone needs medical attention. Tamta began exploring whether a flying vehicle could help people cover such distances faster. His idea was to develop a vehicle that could rise vertically, travel over difficult terrain, and land without needing a runway. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) The aim is to make air travel more accessible in hilly regions, particularly during medical emergencies and in areas that are difficult to reach by road. Developed under his venture, Hapida Sky Private Limited, the HAPIDA SKYNeX combines modified, scaled-up multirotor drone technology with an electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) system. In simple terms, it uses the same basic principle that lets a multirotor drone take off and hover, but applies it to a prototype designed to carry a person. Unlike conventional aircraft that need a runway to gain enough speed for take-off, an eVTOL vehicle is designed to lift off and land vertically. This could make the technology particularly relevant to mountainous areas, where finding suitable space for runways can be difficult. How the flying vehicle works HAPIDA SKYNeX uses multiple electric motors and propellers mounted on external arms to generate lift. Working together, these components are designed to raise the vehicle off the ground, sustain a hover, and help control its movement through the air. This multirotor arrangement is similar in principle to the technology used in drones, although scaling it up to carry a person presents additional engineering and safety challenges. The prototype also features a lightweight frame, a cockpit designed for a single pilot and a transparent canopy. Its electric propulsion system is battery-powered, eliminating direct exhaust emissions during operation. From a mobile-charging shoe to a smart walking stick for visually impaired people, Ravi Tamta's earlier inventions also focused on solving practical, everyday problems. Photograph: ( Business Today ) However, its practical flight range, battery endurance, and overall efficiency will depend on factors such as the battery capacity, the vehicle's weight, and the power required to sustain flight. The intended use is short-distance travel across difficult terrain. According to the reported project details, a journey of around 40 kilometres that takes approximately 90 minutes by mountain road could potentially be completed in 10 to 15 minutes by air. This is an intended travel-time goal, rather than a demonstrated operational capability at this stage. Thirteen years of learning through experiments Tamta did not have an engineering degree or access to a fancy laboratory. Instead, he turned to the internet to learn, relying on his parents' support and repeated experiments to develop his idea. Over 13 years, the concept gradually took shape under his venture, Hapida Skynex. The maiden flight was an important step in testing whether his idea could work beyond the drawing board. The single-seater prototype features a lightweight frame, a cockpit for one pilot and a transparent canopy, with multiple electric motors and propellers designed to generate lift. Photograph: ( Influencer Book of World Records ) The prototype is still at an early stage and requires further testing. While the test flight offers a glimpse of what the vehicle might eventually do, it is too soon to know how it will perform in regular use. Before a vehicle of this kind can be used for routine passenger travel, it would need to demonstrate reliable flight control, sufficient battery performance, structural stability and safe responses to component failures. Operating in mountainous terrain would bring additional considerations, including changing weather, wind conditions, landing-site availability and emergency procedures. From everyday inventions to flying vehicles The flying vehicle is not Tamta's first attempt at solving practical problems through invention. His earlier creations include shoes that charge mobile phones on the go, a smart walking stick for visually impaired people, a bamboo-splitting machine and firefighting equipment. Ravi Tamta hopes HAPIDA SKYNeX will one day make travel across Uttarakhand's mountains faster and more accessible. Photograph: ( Instagram/@ravi_tamta3 ) Each project began with a practical challenge, leading him to explore how a device could make a task easier. HAPIDA SKYNeX has a longer journey ahead before it can carry passengers or help people reach hospitals faster. For now, its first flight marks a step forward for an idea shaped by life in the mountains. As conversations about flying cars continue online, Tamta's work offers a different way to look at the technology: not just as a futuristic mode of transport, but as a possible answer to the everyday challenges of getting from one place to another. Sources: 'Uttarakhand Man Conducts Test Flight Of Drone-Based Flying Vehicle: Watch' by NDTV, Published on 8 August 2026. 'This Uttarakhand youth built an electric flying vehicle. Here's why everyone is talking about Ravi Tamta' by The Times of India, Published on 7 August 2026.

items.titleOriginal: The Call is Real
items.description: Ο Emanuel Kuntzelman έχει ιδιαίτερη σχέση με τα δέντρα. Καθισμένος σε μια μηλιά σε ηλικία έξι ετών, αποφάσισε να αφιερώσει τη ζωή του στην υπηρεσία του σύμπαντος. Κάτω από μια βελανιδιά στο κολέγιο, διατύπωσε μια ιδέα για να ενώσει τους ανθρώπους σε έναν κοινό σκοπό. Διαβάζοντας κάτω από μια ιτιά που κλαίει, του ήρθε το όνομα Holomovement για αυτόν τον κοινό σκοπό, ένα κίνημα…
items.descriptionOriginal: Emanuel Kuntzelman has a special relationship with trees. Sitting in an apple tree at the early age of six, he decided to dedicate his life to serving the universe. Under an oak in college, he formulated an idea to unite people in a common purpose. Reading under a weeping willow, the name Holomovement came to him for that common purpose, a movement he later helped realize. People also appeared along the way as if on cue to point him in a direction when he didn’t know which way he was going. “Sometimes the universe makes things so easy for us — if you're on that quest for truth, and you're willing to say it here and there.” Emanuel believes each person has a calling, a purpose, and trees and people are there to help us as long as we keep learning and seeking. In doing so, all can join in the Holomovement “to unite humanity through our collective purpose.”

items.titleOriginal: Fall nostalgia: why your nervous system reaches for reruns when autumn arrives
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST DAILY Κάθε φθινόπωρο, κάτι συμβαίνει στο σώμα πριν συμβεί στο μυαλό. Η μυρωδιά του καπνού του ξύλου που παρασύρεται μέσα από ένα ραγισμένο παράθυρο, το ιδιαίτερο βάρος του φωτός του Οκτωβρίου που γέρνει στο πάτωμα, και ξαφνικά βρίσκεστε κάπου αλλού εντελώς, πίσω σε μια κουζίνα που δεν έχετε σκεφτεί εδώ και χρόνια ή αισθάνεστε τεταρτημένοι…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Every fall, something happens in the body before it happens in the mind. The smell of wood smoke drifting through a cracked window, the particular weight of October light slanting across the floor, and suddenly you’re somewhere else entirely, back in a kitchen you haven’t thought about in years, or feeling fourteen again for no apparent reason. Then you reach for the show you always watch this time of year, or the book with the cracked spine, and the evening softens. If that pull toward the familiar feels like something you should probably resist, it isn’t. Mental health professionals describe what happens each autumn as a predictable response to something real: the season changing registers in your nervous system as a small form of loss. The nostalgia that follows isn’t a distraction from fall; rather, it’s a part of how you move through it. Seasonal transitions are a form of small loss “Transitions mean something is changing, and change inherently means something is being lost,” says Janna Sayfie , L.M.S.W., co-founder and psychotherapist at Urban Mind Psychotherapy. “These ‘endings,’ however small, register to us as a form of loss. Looking back at something familiar anchors us to a sense of continuity and stability that we try to find when it feels like the ground is shifting beneath us.” That sense of loss takes different shapes for different people. For a lot of adults, the end of summer is the end of a looser way of moving through the week, a rhythm that’s harder to hold onto once September arrives. For parents, back-to-school season carries a weight that’s difficult to articulate, the passage of time made suddenly visible. And even without children in the picture, fall tends to settle in with a certain pressure attached: fresh starts implied, intentions expected, a vague sense that you should be doing more with the season than you are. Matt Sosnowsky , L.C.S.W., founder and psychotherapist at Philadelphia Talk Therapy, compares it to New Year’s, with all the same weight and none of the festivities. Your body recognizes fall before your brain does Part of why autumn nostalgia can feel so sudden and strange is that it often bypasses the thinking mind entirely. Sarah Haugh , L.M.H.C., founder of North Shore Professional Therapy, describes these as somatic memories: body-based recall that surfaces through sensory cues before any conscious recognition has kicked in. “Even before we know what these triggers remind us of, we’re swept away into visceral or nervous system memory,” Haugh says. She explains that this kind of implicit memory, a felt sense rather than a story you can retrieve, is the same part of the memory system that holds experiences from before we had language. Fall is unusually thick with these triggers. Wood smoke through a cracked window. The low angle of October light that somehow reads as different from September even when the temperature hasn’t shifted. Damp leaves, a candle you only bring out once a year, the sound of a school bus on a Tuesday morning. Any of these can pull a decade-old feeling into your chest before you’ve had a chance to ask where it came from. Why reruns feel better than something new Once the nervous system has registered the season as a kind of ending, it tends to steer toward the known. Sayfie puts it plainly: “Our brains tend to favor the predictable over the unpredictable.” We associate the unknown with risk, and when things are shifting, even in the small seasonal way they do every year, the familiar offers something new experiences can’t: you already know how it ends. Revisiting a favorite show or book is one way of meeting that need without quite naming it. The characters feel like company you trust. There’s no uncertainty about whether it will be good. Sosnowsky describes this as a form of safety-seeking, not a failure to engage with what’s ahead, but a way of steadying yourself so that you can. Nostalgia as a tool, not just a feeling Sosnowsky calls nostalgia “an engine for positive emotions,” pointing to research showing that wellbeing draws from three sources: anticipating the future, savoring the present, and looking back at the past. “Taking time to sink into a memory with gratitude and appreciation can help us elevate seminal experiences of joy, connection, and deep meaning,” he says. Nostalgia works that third channel. Don’t think of it as wallowing but as a return to something that still has something to give. Sometimes it carries grief alongside the warmth, which is its own kind of usefulness. A young person packing for college while their mind keeps wandering back to high school. A parent watching a kid start middle school while some part of them is still at kindergarten drop-off. Someone moving through a first round of holidays without a person they love. Looking backward in these moments isn’t getting stuck; it’s how the past gets processed. “Looking back, though sometimes difficult, helps us to integrate our past and make meaning from life,” Sosnowsky says. “In this way, we benefit from the people, places, and experiences that helped shape our lives by recognizing what remains a part of us as we move forward.” So when October settles in, and you find yourself scrolling down to the same playlist, reaching for the same worn-out novel, or clicking on the same show you’ve already seen more times than you can count, that pull isn’t something to override. It may be your nervous system holding onto who you are while the season changes around you. Remind yourself that you can gift yourself that return. At some point, when you’re ready, you can always put something new on. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Fall nostalgia: why your nervous system reaches for reruns when autumn arrives first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The world’s tallest wind turbine just reached full height in Germany. GICON ‘s pilot turbine in Schipkau, eastern Germany, now stands 365 meters (1,197 feet) tall from base to blade tip, making it Germany’s second-tallest structure after Berlin’s TV tower . Official commissioning is set for November. Higher altitude, stronger winds Higher up, winds are faster and more reliable. That translates to more hours of generation per year, and GICON says its design could produce roughly twice the electricity of a conventional turbine with the same rotor diameter. One thing to flag: that’s a claim about cumulative generation over time, not rated power. The turbine’s rated capacity is 3.8 megawatts; future versions are designed to go past seven. The rotor hub sits 300 meters (984 feet) above the ground. Building that high required rethinking construction. A crane capable of reaching 1,197 feet wasn’t realistic, so GICON used a telescoping tower instead. A specialized lifting system raised an inner tower through a surrounding lattice structure, then locked it at full extension. “365 meters – this is an overwhelming moment for our entire team,” said GICON founder and CEO Jochen Großmann. “What was long a challenging idea and then an equally challenging construction project now stands as a globally unique facility in Schipkau.” A second tier for existing wind farms GICON and its funder, Germany’s Federal Agency for Disruptive Innovation (SPRIND), aren’t pitching these turbines as replacements for existing wind farms. The plan is to stack them above. A “second tier” of tall turbines with their rotors spinning above those of conventional turbines already in the ground, adding generation without touching any new land. Germany’s existing wind farms could potentially fit up to 4,000 of them, per the companies’ own estimate. That’s a significant amount of added capacity without a single new wind farm permit. The Schipkau turbine is still a pilot, and the yield projections haven’t been proven in operation yet. GICON and SPRIND are in talks with wind energy companies about commercialization, with series production as the goal. Everything depends on what the numbers look like once it’s running. items.descriptionOriginal: A married California couple has made it their mission to photograph all 40 wild cat species on Earth — and they only have one more to go. The stunning images serve to raise awareness about the animals, many of which are vulnerable or endangered. So far, Sebastian Kennerknecht and Rachel Tobias have traveled to 33 countries across five continents and photographed 39 species in the Felidae family, often using camera traps in forests, deserts, and grasslands where the elusive cats roam. SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht The San Francisco-based duo has captured images of a cheetah in Tanzania, a tiger in India, and an ocelot in Panama. The only species they have yet to cross off the list is the northern oncilla, found in Central America. It’s a rarely seen animal, and one of smallest wild cats in the Americas. View this post on Instagram Kennerknecht, 41, has been photographing cats since college: He studied ecology at the University of California, Santa Cruz, to understand animals and became particularly interested in bobcats. Tobias, 37, grew up loving wildlife and was always drawn to the ocean and photography. The two met online, and they instantly connected over their love of nature. Fittingly, their first date was searching for bobcats. SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht In 2024, Kennerknecht realized he had photos of 30 of the world’s wild cats, so he and Tobias decided to go for the full 40. In addition to photography, the couple run cat expeditions together, taking out small groups to observe the felines in their natural habitat and learn how to photograph them. They’ve raised hundreds of thousands of dollars through their work. One photo of a Borneo Bay cat brought in $120,000 for conservation efforts, and they collected around $70,000 per year for five years to protect lion species in Zambia’s Kafue National Park. They are partnered with Panthera, the world’s leading wild cat conservation organization. Kennerknecht told Talk to the Press that the couple’s work is “99% frustration and 1% joy,” noting that they’ve seen elephants crush their expensive camera traps, insects get into them, and humidity fog up lenses, rendering images unusable. “We set up a studio in the forest,” Tobias explained, adding: “In Malaysia, we set up six traps; we had to sleep in the jungle full of bugs and carry 60 pounds of gear.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht Despite the project’s challenges, the couple is dedicated to ethical photography. They don’t use any bait or lures to attract the cats towards the cameras, so they can observe their natural behavior. “It’s much more successful for telling a story about the species,” said Tobias. “Telling a story between the viewer and the animal is really powerful for conservation.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht A large part of their aim is to introduce the world to the 33 small wild cat species that are relatively unknown, so more can be done to protect them. “If you protect small cats, you protect big cats,” she added. The pair also wants to prove humans can coexist with big and small wild cats. “There are lots of human activities that might negatively impact cats without people knowing,” Tobias said. “People want to protect natural spaces and help with coexistence.” View this post on Instagram In Paraguay at the time of this writing, the team has had camera traps set up since April to capture the northern oncilla, with a ground crew frequently checking on them, but the cat has remained elusive. View this post on Instagram “It’s been pretty incredible,” Kennerknecht said, “but measuring local awareness has been tough.” They’ve set up billboards in areas with wild cats, featuring pictures of the local cats with the slogan, “I’m your neighbor.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht As for their favorite species, Kennerknecht said his is a bobcat, as that’s the feline that launched his photographic journey in Santa Cruz. But for Tobias: “There’s nothing more beautiful than a female leopard.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht Below are the cats they’ve photographed so far: Lion — Zambia Jaguar — Brazil Tiger — India Snow Leopard — Kyrgyzstan Leopard — Zambia Mainland Clouded Leopard — Malaysia Sunda Clouded Leopard — Malaysia African Golden Cat — Uganda Caracal — Yemen Serval — Tanzania Geoffroy’s Cat — Argentina Southern Oncila — Brazil Andean Mountain Cat- Argentina Pampas Cat- Bolivia Ocelot — Panama Margay — Panama Marbled Cat — Malaysia Borneo Bay Cat — Malaysia Asiatic Golden Cat — Indonesia Bobcat — U.S. Canada Lynx — Canada Eurasian Lynx — Kyrgyzstan Iberian Lynx — Spain Mountain Lion — Chile Cheetah — Tanzania Mainland Leopard Cat — Malaysia Sunda Leopard Cat — Malaysia Flat-Headed Cat — Malaysia Rusty-Spotted Cat — India Fishing Cat — Thailand Pallas’s Cat — Mongolia Jungle Cat — India Sand Cat — Western Sahara Black-footed Cat — South Africa European Wild Cat — Spain Afro-Asiatic Wild Cat — Botswana Chinese Mountain Cat — China Jaguarundi — Location Unconfirmed/South America Güiña — Location Unconfirmed/Chile/Argentina This article was originally written by William Ormes Roder for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: Life is a little easier now for a southern ground hornbill in the Netherlands, thanks to 3D-printed prostheses for his upper and lower beak. The turkey-sized bird at the ARTIS Amsterdam Royal Zoo suffered a severe injury that broke both sections of his bill and left him with two stumps, making it difficult for him to pick up food and groom himself. “He managed reasonably well with them, but he could no longer do everything a hornbill naturally does,” ARTIS veterinarian Martine van Zijll Langhout said in a press release . To improve his well-being, the team perfected custom prostheses that are “virtually identical” to his original beak. “A bird uses its beak all day long, to pick up food and, for example, to preen its plumage. Especially with a young bird that can still live to a very old age, we felt it was important to see if we could improve its quality of life,” van Zijll Langhout added. ARTIS Although several birds have been fitted with artificial beaks, this hornbill is believed to be the first to receive replacements for both the upper and lower beak. Should the beak parts continue to function well for the long-term, the team plans to publish a scientific paper detailing exactly how they created the prostheses, so veterinarians around the world can help similar patients. The process is technically complex, as every bird has a unique beak that perfectly aligns to its skull and other anatomy. If the shape isn’t exactly right for either part of the bill, the animal will struggle to use the prosthesis. To ensure their creation would be a success, van Zijll Langhout and her colleagues performed a CT scan of the bird’s head as well as the broken beak pieces. The prostheses were then 3D-printed from plastic, and orthopedic surgeons meticulously attached them using titanium components. View this post on Instagram One of the biggest risks with a procedure like this is that the bird will reject the new beak, which could result in the animal refusing to eat. The zoo staff planned for that possibility and were prepared to have the prostheses removed if need be — but so far, all is going well: The team reported the bird settled in right away after the beak attachment operation and even appeared to be “smiling” afterward . And the day following the surgery, he began eating independently. “That was an incredibly important moment for us,” said van Zijll Langhout. “He understood that he could use his beak and began to discover for himself what was possible with it.” RELATED: From a Dolphin’s Tail to a Bird’s Beak: 7 Innovative Prosthetics That Have Helped Animals

items.descriptionOriginal: The treatment delivers a light-sensitive algae protein to the retina. Paired with special goggles, it can restore limited vision and lasts for years. The patients sit perfectly still as a needle inches toward one of their eyes. After the injection, they’ll no longer be completely human. The syringe is filled with a gene therapy that installs a light-sensitive algae protein into failing retinas and could reboot some lost vision. When scientists first proposed using algae proteins to restore human eyesight, the idea seemed like science fiction. Could alien proteins integrate into our intricate visual system? Even if they did, could the brain translate the resulting signals into sight, rather than nonsensical bursts of light? A new study suggests yes, with caveats. The team treated people with retinitis pigmentosa, a genetic disease that gradually destroys light-sensing cells in the retina. Seven of ten patients showed improved light sensitivity. After patients donned goggles that deliver pulses of light to activate the algae proteins, the team tested their eyesight. Roughly half could reach for and touch objects or identify the orientation of a black bar, a common test of visual recovery. The treatment is still far from restoring full vision. What patients saw was too blurry and the field of view too narrow to discern texture or fine detail. The boundaries of objects looked squiggly. But those who responded to the treatment continued to improve over roughly five years. One participant, whose story made headlines in 2021 , can now recognize and count different objects, and white stripes on a crosswalk pop out. The study, called PIONEER , is an ambitious clinical trial combining gene therapy with optogenetics. The first goal was to assess safety, and it met the mark. Most participants experienced a brief bout of inflammation in the eye receiving the injection. The only patient to suffer a severe side effect was quickly treated with medication. The findings suggest the initial success wasn’t a fluke. The study “represents an important milestone for optogenetic vision restoration,” said study author Stefan Futterknecht at the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel, in a press release . Setting Sights High Around two decades ago, Karl Deisseroth was hunting for new ways to control brain cells. Electrical bursts and chemicals, which are how neurons communicate, seemed like obvious choices. But nature had something stranger to offer: algae. Algae produce a protein called channelrhodopsin. When activated by light, the protein changes neuron activity using a mechanism that works similarly in mammalian cells. In a foundational paper , Deisseroth’s team inserted the protein into rodent neurons, and voilá—the neurons could now be controlled using light. The technology, called optogenetics, revolutionized neuroscience. By genetically tagging specific neurons with channelrhodopsin, scientists can now dial the cells’ activity up or down like a dimmer switch. Optogenetic experiments have revealed brain circuits that shape feelings, memory, and cognition with unprecedented precision. Researchers panning for more genes in different algae strains struck gold again. One channelrhodopsin variant they found, ChrimsonR, was particularly exciting. Unlike the classic version that’s activated by blue light, ChrimsonR responds to amber light, which penetrates tissues better and is less damaging. More recently, scientists have begun to use generative AI to redesign natural proteins to make them even more sensitive to light. “Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, when the technology won the coveted prize this year. Still, it has mainly been considered a research tool. Light It Up Retinitis pigmentosa gradually robs people of their eyesight. Researchers have linked over 100 genetic variations to the condition, which kills off light-sensitive cells in the retina. “The replacement (or editing) of a single gene would not help most persons,” wrote Deisseroth in the New England Journal of Medicine . Instead, adding channelrhodopsin could offer a more universal solution by rewiring surviving neurons. Early successes bolstered the idea. In one study , scientists equipped cones—a type of retinal light-sensing cell—with channelrhodopsin in mice with retinitis pigmentosa. The therapy boosted their light sensitivity. It also reactivated cones that had stopped responding to light in human retina samples. The new study took a different approach. In advanced disease, cones may have already degenerated beyond the point at which they could be saved. So instead, the gene therapy targeted ganglion cells. These cells process signals from light-sensitive cells and pass that information to the brain, but don’t detect light themselves. Ganglion cells are, however, more resilient than cones. Add channelrhodopsin, and they could become substitute light sensors. The team packed genetic instructions for ChrimsonR into a harmless viral delivery system and injected it into the poorer seeing eye of 10 patients aged 40 to 73. All were legally blind, and each received one of three escalating doses. As the patients gradually built up levels of the algae protein in their eyes, the team faced another challenge: Translating visual scenes from the outside world into amber light that the engineered ganglion cells could recognize. They developed specialized goggles that look a bit like Apple’s Vision Pro. The goggles use a camera to scan the field of view thousands of times per second, monitoring for light changes in every pixel. When the device detects a change, it pulses amber light from that pixel into the eye. Because our eyes naturally dart around—often without us noticing—this dynamic method may better mimic normal vision. With the goggles on, 6 of 10 participants showed clinically meaningful improvement in light sensitivity, with more than a fourfold boost over baseline readings. One participant improved over 62-fold. Of the eight who agreed to further eyesight tests, roughly half could touch a notebook, grab a small staple box, and detect changes in a rotating bar. Of those who initially responded to the treatment, improvements lasted for years. Their brains also seemed to adapt to the alien light sensors. In one test, participants were asked to open or close their eyes while looking at a tumbler. Electrical brain signals related to vision were more coherent with eyes open, suggesting their perception depended on improved visual input. Any gene therapy carries risk. In an already worsening eye, inflammation and other side effects could cause further damage. Overall, the injection appeared relatively safe. Most participants experienced a temporary increase in eye pressure, but no detectable side effects throughout the body. The retina’s overall structure remained unchanged. One person suffered a blockage in a major eye artery that cleared within minutes after treatment with an FDA-approved eye drop. For now, the participants still can’t read or see faces. The therapy reaches only a fraction of their ganglion cells, making sharper vision harder to restore. More advanced versions of channelrhodopsin with greater light sensitivity may increase resolution. As for the hardware, the team is working on versions of the goggles that deliver more accurate and timely stimulation. Potential upgrades include an eye tracker, software to preprocess visual scenes, and even holographs . “Overall, although optogenetic methods have been developed primarily for basic science discovery,” wrote Deisseroth, they’re now heading towards “diverse therapeutic approaches.” The post Blind Patients Recover Partial Vision in Gene Therapy Trial appeared first on SingularityHub .

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers in Spain have shown that a modular tire in which tread and casing are designed as separate pieces stays together while in use, provided that it’s properly inflated. “This is an encouraging step toward a more sustainable tire architecture, where the worn tread could potentially be replaced while the main tire structure is reused,” says study team member Farshad Afshari , a PhD researcher at Universidad Carlos III de Madrid (UC3M) and Universidad Politécnica de Madrid (UPM).. A modular automobile tire could be easier to recycle compared to conventional ones, which require time- and labor-intensive separation of rubber treads and sidewalls from steel belts and bead cores. It would also use materials more efficiently, since there would be less material to replace at any given time. A modular tire could also be better for the environment . Conventional rubber tires are a prominent source of microplastic pollution because tiny rubber particles degrade due to friction and enter the air and waterways. But the modular design could open up the possibility of making each component of the tire from safer and more easily recyclable materials. It’s a compelling idea in theory, but would the components of a modular tire actually stay together in practice? Afshari and his collaborators built a scaled-down prototype of their ECOTIRE modular tire concept, in which tread and casing are mechanically interlocked through a series of bumps and hollows like the two halves of a waffle iron. They tested the tire on a custom-built rolling test rig in the lab to see how the tire would fare while varying parameters such as load, turning radius, inflation pressure, and slip. At normal inflation pressure, the tire’s components stayed together under all conditions tested. But at half the normal pressure, the tread and casing could separate, especially under a combination of high load, tight rolling radius, and greater slip conditions. The researchers tested the tire for over 12,000 revolutions, equivalent to more than 7 kilometers. At the end of the experiment there was no indication of wear and tear on the tread or the rest of the tire—promising albeit preliminary evidence of the tire’s durability. In the prototype, both tread and casing are made from silicone rubber, but the researchers anticipate using a different material in eventual manufactured tires. “The next major steps include developing full-scale prototypes using materials representative of commercial tires and evaluating their performance under more realistic driving conditions,” Afshari reports. “This would involve braking and traction forces, transient maneuvers, temperature variations, road irregularities, and long-term fatigue and wear.” Head-to-head tests with conventional tires will be another key milestone further down the road. Source: García-Pozuelo D. et al . “ Measurement of rolling stability and slip angle effects on a modular ECOTIRE .” Measurement 2026. Image: ©Anthropocene Magazine.

items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία δημοσιεύτηκε αρχικά από το The Understory. Όταν ήμουν φοιτήτρια στο Πανεπιστήμιο Cornell, διάβασα το βιβλίο «Fraternity Gang Rape» της Peggy Reeves Sanday για μια από τις τάξεις μου. Αυτό το βιβλίο γράφτηκε το 1990, που ήταν πολύ καιρό πριν. Αλλά και πάλι, ήταν; Σήμερα έβγαλα το βιβλίο από το ράφι μου. Ξεφυλλίζοντας το, παρατήρησα ένα νοσηρό patte…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story was originally published by The Understory . W hen I was a student at Cornell University, I read the book “Fraternity Gang Rape” by Peggy Reeves Sanday for one of my classes. That book was written in 1990, which was a long time ago. But then again, was it? I took the book off my shelf today. Paging through it, I noticed a sickening pattern. Parts of it felt ripped from the allegations coming out of the Cornell investigation today: Long nights saturated in alcohol. Women who spend days tunneling through layers of self-blame and shame before concluding they’ve been raped. Prosecutors who do not pursue charges. One example: a 19-year-old woman at a small Midwestern college drank alcohol, had sex with her boyfriend, “fell asleep and the next thing she knew she awoke with a man she didn’t know on top of her.” The more things change, apparently, the less any goddamn thing changes. But wait. At moments of despair like this, I have learned to stop and ask myself: Is it actually true that nothing has changed? There has been some extraordinary reporting done about the Cornell case, including by The Cornell Daily Sun , the student-run newspaper that gave me my first reporting job many years ago. But as usually happens with terrifying news stories, it’s very hard to figure out how to assess the threat — and find proven solutions. How typical was this case? Is sexual assault happening more or less over time? In other words, what is the denominator for whatever fresh horror we are worried about? Most importantly, what actually works to make sexual assault more rare? Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] To answer these questions, I’m going to uncomfortably set aside many other important questions — about accountability, humanity, legality, fairness and barbarity. Those are questions being interrogated in many other places. Here at The Understory, we’re trying to fill gaps that we see in traditional journalism. And one of those gaps is almost always context: How often are horrible things happening, and what can be done to make them more rare? These are the kinds of questions that we know humans need answered, in order to stay sane and take meaningful action in a time of relentless news battering us from near and far. So in that spirit, here is what I have learned so far: Rape reports have been declining in the U.S. since 2021. For 2025, the FBI estimates that 36 rape offenses were reported for every 100,000 people. The number of rapes that get reported to law enforcement each year has been gradually declining every year since 2021 , based on FBI data. This data comes with giant caveats, though. First, the number of actual sexual assaults is far higher than the number that get reported. (Only about 24 percent of sexual assaults were reported to authorities in 2024, according to the National Crime Victimization Survey .) Second, the FBI broadened its definition of rape in 2013, so it is hard to compare statistics going back any further than that. (The current definition includes “penetration, no matter how slight, of the vagina or anus with any body part or object, or oral penetration by a sex organ of another person, without the consent of the victim.”) In general, definitions of rape and sexual assault vary from place to place, making it harder than it should be to track changes over time and to find which cities, states or countries have unusually low (or high) rates. Sexual assault remains appallingly common on college campuses. In 2019, 13 percent of college students reported that they’d experienced some form of sexual assault since they’d arrived on campus. This category is broader than the FBI definition of rape; it includes nonconsensual penetration, attempted penetration, sexual touching by force or inability to consent. This data comes from the 181,752 students who responded to the 2019 Campus Climate Survey (conducted by the Association of American Universities). Importantly, the odds vary tremendously depending on who you are. The rate of sexual assault for women and transgender or nonbinary students was 20 percent — or four times the rate for men. Credit: Zhuoyao Song / Shutterstock The Cornell case is typical in some ways. In most campus sexual assaults, both the victim and the offender have consumed alcohol or drugs. Typically, rape victims are girls and very young women, and the vast majority of perpetrators are male. Victims usually know their perpetrators. At colleges, assaults primarily happen in residences or fraternity houses, according to the Campus Climate Survey (and Cornell’s own 2025 survey on sexual assault). And if a victim reports the offense, official responses are slow and unsatisfying, generally speaking. In all these ways, the Cornell case seems fairly typical. The Cornell case is atypical in other ways. Most sexual assault cases involve just one perpetrator, not multiple, making the Cornell allegations unusual. The other rarity is that the woman in this case reported the incident. And she has continued to push for a reckoning in a civil suit filed this year. To date, none of the accused men has been charged with a crime, and all have denied wrongdoing. Something can be done. And is being done. There is a lot of speculation happening right now about what leads to rape. Can we blame always-accessible, violent porn? Or campus hookup culture and frat-boy privilege? I have hunches about this, like everyone else. But I’m more interested in evidence of change. What actually works to reduce the number of rapes? And guess what? We now have some answers — answers we did not have when I was a student at Cornell. A 2014 study led by Laura Salazar at Georgia State University randomly assigned 743 college men to receive something called the RealConsent online training or a generic online health program. RealConsent featured six 30-minute modules about informed consent, intimate communication skills, the role of alcohol and male socialization in sexual violence, empathy for rape victims and bystander education. Six months later, the men who had received the special training reported intervening more often to stop a peer from engaging in sexually violent or inappropriate behavior. And, most importantly, they reported engaging in less sexual aggression themselves. “The odds for perpetrating among RealConsent participants were 73 percent lower than participants in the comparison condition,” according to the study. The attitudes of these men changed, too. They had greater empathy for rape victims, less hostility toward women and less comfort with other men’s inappropriate behaviors. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Another program, which has been studied even more extensively, first appeared in The New England Journal of Medicine in 2015. The researchers, led by Charlene Senn at the University of Windsor, randomly assigned a group of first-year female students at three Canadian universities to receive a special training program for resisting sexual assault. The control group got general brochures on sexual assault instead. The training program, known as EAAA (for Enhanced Assess, Acknowledge, Act) featured four three-hour sessions. Students were taught how to assess risk, overcome emotional barriers in acknowledging danger and engage in effective verbal and physical self-defense. In all, 451 women received the EAAA training, and 442 women got the brochures. One year later, the researchers checked in on the women. Get this: women in the training group were 46 percent less likely to report having been raped than women in the control group. They were also 63 percent less likely to report attempted rapes. A subsequent study found that the benefits continued, even two years later. “The program significantly reduced the risk of completed and attempted rape, attempted coercion, and nonconsensual sexual contact over the entire follow-up period,” the study concluded, “yielding reductions between 30 percent and 64 percent at 2 years.” Women who still became victims of sexual violence, despite the training, were less likely to blame themselves than women in the control group. The U.S. Air Force Academy has adopted the program for first-year female cadets. So have many colleges, including Stanford University. Interestingly, Cornell University has tried out this program, too. Cornell facilitators piloted the EAAA program in 2019 and 2020. Then the pandemic came along and on-campus training stopped . Which means it’s unlikely that the students involved in the 2024 case got this training. Last year, Cornell revived the EAAA program with sorority members, as well as a parallel program for fraternity members. You might wonder: Why isn’t every high school student getting proven training like this? There are many reasons, but one reason is that too few people know about these options. When rapes get covered in the media, the reporting almost never includes research like this. It can feel like this kind of violence is inevitable — or the fault of some inherent flaw in the perpetrators. But violence is never inevitable. We, as a society, tend to focus on holding perpetrators accountable after the fact. And this is important, but tragically late. It would be great if laws were clearer, data collection was consistent and police and prosecutors had excellent, trauma-informed training. But it would be infinitely better to prevent more rapes from happening at all. “Despair demands less of us, it’s more predictable, and in a sad way safer,” Rebecca Solnit wrote in Hope in the Dark. “Authentic hope requires clarity — seeing the troubles in this world — and imagination, seeing what might lie beyond these situations that are perhaps not inevitable and immutable.” The post There Are Ways to Reduce Campus Sexual Assaults. Will More Colleges Use Them? appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: When Daniel Zhang was nine, he watched his grandmother lose her hair to chemotherapy and couldn't understand why medicine could look so much like harm. That confusion never left him, and when his grandfather was later diagnosed with cancer -- and Zhang saw the same bewilderment on his seven-year-old sister's face -- it became the seed of something purposeful. He and his classmate Zachary Tou, both 17, built *Tumor Tactics*, a Pok mon-inspired card game that teaches children cancer biology through the same mechanics they already love -- where, as Zhang explains, "chemotherapy can be a really powerful treatment, but you have to roll a die to determine how effective it is, and you might have to skip your next turn to recover from its side effects." What began as one boy trying to translate grief into language a child could hold has grown into a student-led nonprofit running workshops across San Diego schools, reaching kids from kindergarten through eighth grade. Perhaps most quietly remarkable is what happens at the end of each session: Zhang and Tou open the floor for discussion, and children -- unbidden -- begin sharing their own family stories, needing not just explanation, but the invitation to be heard.

items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο γράφτηκε από τον Peter McGraw, καθηγητή μάρκετινγκ και ψυχολογίας στο Πανεπιστήμιο του Colorado Boulder, για το The Conversation — έναν μη κερδοσκοπικό ειδησεογραφικό οργανισμό αφιερωμένο στην ανταλλαγή γνώσεων ερευνητών και επιστημόνων, με άδεια Creative Commons. Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Τα σόλο ταξίδια αυξάνονται — και μια βιομηχανία…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Peter McGraw , a professor of marketing and psychology at the University of Colorado Boulder, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . Solo travel is surging — and an industry still largely built for two is taking note. Google reported in April 2026 that online searches involving “solo travel” hit an all-time high this year, with queries for “women solo travel” reaching a 15-year peak. Hilton’s 2026 trends report found that 26% of travelers planned to take a trip alone this year, and that nearly half said they planned to add solo days to the front or back of a family trip. The issue isn’t new. In 1992, marketing researchers identified the solo consumer as an underserved market . But as tourism researchers have documented , the accommodation sector treats double occupancy as the default unit of consumption, which often slaps a “single supplement” charge on customers when they travel without a partner. The industry essentially penalizes travelers for arriving without a second body to fill the other half of a room they aren’t using. The reason why so many hotels, cruise lines, and tour operators still base prices on double occupancy is that their costs — the room, the berth, the coach seat, the guide — don’t fall by half when the second person fails to materialize. But the supplement isn’t just a pricing convention. It’s the clearest signal the industry sends about who it built the product for. I’m a scholar who studies what I call the solo economy : how institutions and markets adapt, or fail to adapt, to the rise of single living. I’ve written before about how retail and restaurants still design for pairs. Travel is further along than most in recognizing this cultural shift. It’s also a useful case because the industry has started on the easy part of the problem but barely touched the rest. Demographics Matter, but Not the Way You’d Think The broader shift toward solo living is real. In 2025, 39.7 million Americans lived alone . That’s 29% of all households, up from 20% in 1975. Married couples, meanwhile, fell to 47% of households from 66% 50 years earlier. Those numbers alone don’t explain solo travel. Some of that decline went to people living alone; some went to unmarried couples, who are still a party of two on a booking page. Married people take trips alone. Single people travel with friends, siblings and parents, and plenty of them have logged serious hours as an extra wheel. Living alone and vacationing alone are different behaviors with different causes. What connects them is the erosion of a single assumption: that every adult arrives with a plus-one. That assumption is weakening at home, and it’s now encountering the booking page. Price Is the Easy Rung One response by the travel industry has been to shave the single supplement. For example, the tour operator Tauck announced this year that it’s waiving the single supplement on a class of its riverboat cabins across more than 250 European river cruise departures and reducing it by up to US$600 on 105 land departures. Another touring company has taken a more committed approach to adjusting its offerings: Aurora Expeditions sets aside 10 dedicated solo cabins on every sailing across its three ships, with no single supplement, through its 2026 and 2027 seasons. Then there’s Norwegian Cruise Line, which was early to the shift. In 2010, it introduced Studio staterooms aboard Norwegian Epic: small cabins designed for one passenger, sold at single-occupancy prices and arranged around a keycard-access Studio Lounge reserved for solo travelers. The trade-off is less private space, but at a price for one, with access to a room full of fellow travelers going it alone. Norwegian then expanded solo categories in 2024 from nine ships to its full 19-ship fleet. But on ships without Studios, much of the expansion was relabeling. Cruise Critic reported that standard double-occupancy rooms would likely be reclassified rather than retrofitted. And by Norwegian’s own account , the Studio Lounge is reserved for guests in Solo Studios — so the fleetwide solo categories come with the discount but not the room full of other solo travelers. That’s the difference between repricing and redesigning. The 2010 Studio was a purpose-built 100-square-foot (9 square-meter) cabin that cost Norwegian something to construct. The 2024 categories are, in many cases, the same rooms as before, with a new label and a discount. The solo traveler pays less than two people would, but it’s still more than half for a room sized and built for two. A cabin sold to one occupies the same space as a cabin sold to two, and the industry still counts berths. There’s a cleaner approach. Yotel sells a room type it calls Solo — 114 square feet (about 10 square meters) in New York City, maximum occupancy one, at the bottom of its price range. Nothing was subtracted to make it. It was built at that size, for that guest, and priced accordingly. That’s what designing for one looks like, and it’s rare enough that a tiny room counts as progress. alvarez—E+/Getty Images Many solo travelers seek control over their experiences and schedules, but they still seek a social component. Traveling Alone Doesn’t Mean Being Alone A common mistake in designing for solo travelers is assuming that solitude is the product. It isn’t. In the same 2026 data showing record interest in solo travel, Google found that searches for “travel groups” and “tour groups” also hit record highs . A Mastercard survey of more than 15,000 consumers across 11 countries found that 39% of international travelers had already taken a trip alone — and 7 in 10 international leisure travelers were interested in solo experiences built to connect them with like-minded people. The contradiction makes sense when you acknowledge that privacy and isolation are two different things. A person can want total control over where to go, when to eat, and when to return to the room — and still want company at dinner. The issue with double-occupancy pricing is that it assumes the customer brings their own company. But when only one person books, the operator has to address the pricing problem — whether or how to discount; and a product problem — how to supply a social component. Waiving a solo supplement solves the first issue, but it ignores the second. Norwegian understood this in 2010 by creating its lounge for solo travelers. The Pitch Is Easier When the Product Is for One For all these changes, travel advertising often still runs on couples: two glasses of wine, two lounge chairs, two silhouettes against a sunset. Sandals Resorts built an entire resort category around the premise. When solo travel does appear, it gets a different script. The traveler is adventurous, on a journey of self-discovery. AARP’s current solo-travel guide emphasizes personal growth and self-reliance. Even Norwegian closes its solo pitch by reassuring the reader that “you’re pretty good company.” The effect is to mark solo travel as exceptional at precisely the moment it stops being exceptional. Nobody reassures a couple that they will enjoy the balcony. Calling a solo traveler “brave” can be a compliment, but it can also reveal the assumption that traveling alone is abnormal, even when that’s changing. That all said, parts of the tourism industry have taken big steps over the past 15 years. But treating solo travelers as an audience rather than an accommodation is harder. It’s about selling them what they have already said they want: control over the trip, and access to other people, on their own terms. Marketing researchers named this opportunity in 1992. Thirty-four years later, the industry is still learning to build for one. Meanwhile, the solo traveler is standing at reception, holding a credit card, waiting for someone to design a room. items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Τα περισσότερα οικοδομικά υλικά έχουν σχεδιαστεί για να αντέχουν τα στοιχεία, να παραμένουν σφραγισμένα και αναλλοίωτα για όσο το δυνατόν περισσότερο. Η Respyre, μια ολλανδική startup, εργάζεται από την αντίθετη αρχή. Η εταιρεία έχει αναπτύξει το Mosscrete, μια βιοδεκτική επίστρωση σκυροδέματος που δημιουργεί τις συνθήκες για να αναπτυχθούν βρύα απευθείας σε κάθετα…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most building materials are designed to resist the elements, to stay sealed and unchanged for as long as possible. Respyre , a Dutch startup, is working from the opposite premise. The company has developed Mosscrete , a bioreceptive concrete coating that creates conditions for moss to grow directly on vertical surfaces, drawing moisture from rain and air without any soil or irrigation system. The science comes from research at Delft University of Technology , and since its commercial launch, Respyre has applied the technology across eight projects in Belgium and the Netherlands. How moss takes hold Moss doesn’t have roots in the conventional sense; it attaches to surfaces through rhizoids, tiny thread-like structures that cling to the material without penetrating or damaging it. Unlike a traditional green wall , which needs structural support for soil, a built-in watering system, and regular upkeep, Mosscrete sidesteps most of that. And because it’s applied as a coating rather than built in, it can go onto an existing facade just as easily as a new one. The material works especially well on blank or inaccessible walls where conventional planting isn’t an option, and Respyre has been using those spaces to test how the technology holds up under different real-world conditions. Eight buildings, different tests In Kortrijk, Belgium, 450 square meters (about 4,840 square feet) of a new industrial warehouse facade were coated with Mosscrete during construction and integrated with rainwater harvesting, keeping the whole system maintenance-free from day one. A 300-square-meter (about 3,230-square-foot) noise barrier in Hoofddorp, the Netherlands, is being used to test passive greening: moss growing from natural moisture alone, no watering involved. The porous structure of moss may also help absorb sound, which makes the noise barrier a natural fit for the technology. A 260-square-meter (about 2,800-square-foot) social housing facade in Purmerend was one of the first practical applications. Traditional greening options were rejected there as too expensive and maintenance-heavy, and the project helped Respyre work out how bioreceptive facades are best designed and applied. In Haarlem, a 313-square-meter (about 3,370-square-foot) commercial renovation combined Mosscrete with insulation, aiming to both green the facade and improve thermal performance. Research published in June 2026 in the journal Science of the Total Environment found the effect is moisture-dependent: wet moss creates a cooling effect through evaporation, while dry moss can overheat in direct sunlight. In Amsterdam, the technology is being tested on bridge piers where graffiti has been a persistent problem. Moss-covered surfaces are less appealing as targets, and since the site has no irrigation, the project is also tracking how moss develops under ordinary conditions of rain, shade, and humidity. Designing for change Respyre is betting on a different idea of what building materials should do. Most are made to resist change, to stay gray and sealed for decades. Mosscrete is made for the opposite: it works best when moss gradually takes over. Urban greening helps manage stormwater and heat in dense cities, and there’s evidence it supports local biodiversity too. But a building slowly covered in moss doesn’t look like neglect. It looks like something is alive there. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post A Dutch startup is making concrete that grows its own moss first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .
